summary: A University of Luxembourg study of whether letting the test generator see LLM-written faulty code weakens fault detection. For each task in HumanEval+, MBPP and BigCodeBench (all Python), each model's hardest faulty solution is kept. Five models (GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B) then write tests with an LLM-Plain loop that repairs compile errors only. Tests written from the task description alone detect more faults than tests that see the code, whether the code is in the prompt or in an earlier turn of the same conversation. The gap is significant for all five models (Mann-Whitney p<0.05), and summarization, CoT and CoVe variants do not close it.

claims.claim: Exposing the implementation under test reduces fault detection of LLM-generated tests
claims.evidence: Fig. 2, Table II: prompt-only vs prompt+code is significant for all 5 models (p≤0.009), a mean drop of 13.2 points. Prompt+code vs code-only is not significant for any model. This replicates earlier work ([5] Huang et al.; [7] same group).

claims.claim: A code-then-test session (the 'agentic workflow') detects fewer faults than test generation in a fresh, spec-only context
claims.evidence: Fig. 4, Table IV: the test-driven arm wins for all 5 models, by 7.9 to 17.7 points (mean 11.7), with p from <0.0001 to 0.0177. Same models, loop and faulty implementations. The number of faulty implementations per model and benchmark is never reported, and Mann-Whitney ignores the paired design.

claims.claim: Fault detection is 14% when tests come after faulty code vs 25% when generated independently
claims.evidence: The absolute levels appear only in the abstract and §I. The body text gives only per-model differences, and the figures carrying absolute values are not in the extracted text. The mean gap (11.7) is consistent with 25 vs 14, but whether '%' means percentage points or relative change is never stated.

claims.claim: Prompting strategies (summarization, CoT, CoVe) do not mitigate the bias
claims.evidence: Table III: all are significantly worse than prompt-only for every model. But these strategies are applied with the code exposed (summarization summarizes the code under test). No spec-only CoT or CoVe arm was run, so code exposure and prompting technique are confounded.

claims.claim: Errors propagate across multi-step agentic workflows
claims.evidence: The 'agentic workflow' is a two-turn chat (write code, then write tests in the same conversation) with no tools and no longer chains. Decomposition into sub-tasks is argued in §I but not measured.

claims.claim: The gap is not explained by test count, coverage or fault triggering, and is likely due to oracle quality
claims.evidence: Tables V and VI and Fig. 5 show CoT and CoVe write more tests and coverage is similar (~95-99%) across arms. Oracle correctness is not measured directly (Finding 4 concedes this).

patterns.note: Independent, spec-only test generation beats tests written after seeing the code, for 5/5 models with the same loop and the same faulty code (Table IV). The tested arm is 'tests independent of implementation', not a full red-green TDD loop, and code was never regenerated against the tests.

An execution-verifier loop that uses tests the same model wrote after seeing its own code is weakened: fault detection falls about 8-18 points. Verifier tests need to come from the spec or a context isolated from the implementation.

Tests derived from the natural-language spec catch more faults than tests derived from code, with the same model and budget. Under-specified MBPP prompts did about as well as the originals (Fig. 6), so the gain comes from independence from the code rather than from richer specs.

Compares two fixed pipelines that differ only in what context the test step receives. Isolating the test step from the implementation wins for all 5 models. This informs how to wire nodes inside a static graph (or a fresh-context subagent). It does not test a workflow graph against a plain agent loop, because the alternative is a single two-turn chat.
§I argues that decomposed sub-task chains propagate upstream errors into downstream steps. Only a two-step code-then-test chain is measured, and no planner-generated DAG is evaluated.

One shared conversation for both implementation and tests propagates the model's own errors into the test oracles. The evidence is narrow (no tools, two turns) and does not bear on single-agent loops in general.

methodology.sample: HumanEval+ (164), MBPP (974) and BigCodeBench (1,140) tasks; per model, 10 solutions per task at T=0.8, keeping one hardest faulty solution (≤50% of reference tests failing). The final number of faulty implementations is not reported.
methodology.baselines: Spec-only LLM-Plain test generation vs code-aware variants (prompt+code, code-only, summarization, CoT, CoVe) and a same-session code-then-test workflow; all use the same model and loop
methodology.models: GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct
methodology.variance: Mann-Whitney U p-values per comparison; no CIs, no per-run variance, no multiple-comparison correction; test generation appears to be a single run at low temperature
methodology.ablations: Prompting strategies; under-specified MBPP prompt variants; diagnostic tables of test count, line coverage and fault triggering
methodology.contamination_controls: None. HumanEval+ and MBPP are widely memorized, which could favor the spec-only arm (the model may recall canonical behavior).

standards.artifacts: No replication package, prompts or generated tests linked; benchmarks are public

biases.detail: Function-level tasks; BigCodeBench is the only one with library-heavy code. The authors acknowledge industrial systems may differ.
HumanEval+ and MBPP reference behavior is likely memorized, which may inflate spec-only oracle quality.
The number of faulty implementations per model and benchmark, which is the unit behind every p-value, is never given.
Mann-Whitney is used on a paired design (same faulty implementation under both arms), with no correction across the 30+ comparisons.
'Agentic' and 'multi-step workflows' are claimed, but the setup is a two-turn chat with a compile-repair loop and no tools.

'We introduce the phenomenon of error propagation', yet [5] and [7] already showed that faulty code in the prompt biases test oracles. Only RQ3 (implicit exposure through the conversation) is new. The paper also cites Huang et al. [27] as finding that faulty code plus the task description improves detection, and does not reconcile that with its own result.
No code, prompts or data released.
No token or call costs per arm.

coi.affiliations: SnT, University of Luxembourg (all three authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Models from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and Meta; no author affiliation with them
coi.detail: Independent academic study. The LLM-Plain baseline is the first author's prior work [13], which is a self-citation, not a commercial interest.

verdict_reason: The direction of the effect is consistent across five models from four providers, three benchmarks and several prompting variants, and it replicates earlier work. The headline absolute numbers (14% vs 25%) are not in the body text, though. Sample sizes are never reported, the statistics ignore pairing, everything is Python function-level with contamination risk, and the 'agentic workflow' is a two-turn chat.
applicability: The lesson is about how steps are wired, which matters whichever structure the team picks. A test or acceptance-check step must get the spec (acceptance criteria), not the implementation or the coding agent's conversation. Code-then-test in one context lost about 8-18 points of fault detection across five models. In a static workflow graph (P36) this is a cheap, enforceable rule: the spec feeds the test node, and code output goes only to the executor. In an LLM-generated DAG (P37) the planner can easily wire the implementation into the test node, so the executor or a qr check should refuse verification nodes whose inputs include the implementation. For the SDD rollout, generate JUnit acceptance tests from the spec before, or independently of, implementation, and do not let the coding agent write its own oracles. Transfer to Java services spanning several repositories is unverified: the evidence is Python function-level work with no repository context.

conflicts_with.detail: Agrees in direction: TDD-Agent's dominant failure is self-written tests and code co-evolving into consistent-but-wrong states.
Agrees in direction: GTDD separates test generation from the coding agent and finds regenerated independent tests beat tests written once by the same LLM.

Tension for Java: CATGen feeds the focal method and project context to the test generator by design. Under this paper's finding, such tests behave as regression oracles that can mirror existing faults. CATGen optimizes compile and coverage rather than fault detection, so the two are complementary, not contradictory.
